mcqs.question: A team is deciding whether to build their own feature-flag system or adopt an existing one. Per this topic, what's the right way to frame the decision?
options: Whether the team is technically capable of building it, since capability alone should decide build vs buy
Whether feature flags are interesting enough to justify in-house engineering effort
Always buy, since building infrastructure in-house is never justified
Whether feature-flag infrastructure is the team's actual differentiator, weighed against the ongoing maintenance burden building it would create versus the ongoing cost of an existing option
mcqs.explanation: "Can we build it" is almost always true and beside the point — the real comparison is total ongoing cost and whether owning this specific system is where the team's differentiation actually comes from. Neither "always buy" nor "is it interesting" nor raw capability is the right frame per this topic.

mcqs.question: A design doc compares two options purely on build cost and latency numbers, with no mention of what happens after launch. What's missing, per this topic?
options: A code sample showing the implementation
Operational burden — the ongoing cost of pages, upgrades, and incident response that doesn't show up until after launch
A cost estimate in a specific currency
A diagram of the system architecture
mcqs.explanation: Operational burden is easy to leave out precisely because it doesn't appear until after launch, yet it's a real, recurring cost — pages, on-call load, upgrades — that should be estimated in the doc up front. Code samples, currency-specific figures, and diagrams aren't the gap this topic is pointing at.

mcqs.question: A build-in-house option looks cheaper than a managed service when comparing only the initial build cost. What does total cost of ownership add to this comparison?
options: Nothing — initial build cost is the only number that matters for a fair comparison
Only the licensing fee of the managed alternative
The run and maintain costs summed over the design's realistic lifetime, which often make build-in-house more expensive over 2-3 years despite a cheaper start
A discount applied to whichever option the team prefers
mcqs.explanation: Total cost of ownership sums build, run, and maintain cost over the design's realistic lifetime — build-in-house commonly starts cheaper but its run and maintain costs grow each year, flipping the comparison by year two or three. Comparing only initial build cost is exactly the mistake this topic warns against.

mcqs.question: Per this topic's comparison, when should you pick the theoretically "correct" design over the one this team can actually operate?
options: Always — technical correctness should override operational fit
Never — the team's current ability should always be the deciding factor regardless of the gap
Only if the design doc looks more impressive to reviewers
When the gap between the two is small enough that the team can realistically grow into the more optimal design before that gap matters
mcqs.explanation: The topic's guidance is to state both designs explicitly and default to the one the team can operate, choosing the theoretically ideal option only when the team can plausibly grow into it before the gap becomes a real problem. Neither an absolute "always" nor an absolute "never" nor doc aesthetics reflect that guidance.

mcqs.question: A team picks a newer, more interesting database over a boring, well-understood one mainly because it's more technically exciting. What's the risk this topic identifies?
options: The team may hit undocumented failure modes it has no experience with, burning time relearning lessons the boring alternative already had answers for
Newer databases are always slower in benchmarks
This choice is risk-free as long as the database is popular in the industry
The main risk is that the vendor might raise prices later
mcqs.explanation: "More interesting" and "the right fit for this team" are unrelated properties — an unfamiliar system's operational unknowns can cost real time in production, regardless of its technical merits or popularity. Benchmark speed and future vendor pricing aren't the risk this topic is naming.
